prompt: What makes an acetylide anion strongly nucleophilic?

choices.text: The negative charge and unshared electron pair on carbon
A vacant p orbital on the sp-hybridized carbon
choices.why: A vacant orbital makes a species an electron-pair acceptor, an electrophile, like a carbocation.

choices.text: The positive polarization of its terminal carbon atom
choices.why: A positively polarized carbon is electrophilic, like the carbon of bromomethane that the acetylide attacks.

choices.text: Its weakness as a base, so it never removes protons
choices.why: Acetylide ions are strong bases, strong enough to cause elimination with secondary and tertiary alkyl halides.

explanation: The negative charge and unshared electron pair on carbon make an acetylide anion strongly nucleophilic. As a result, it can react with electrophiles such as alkyl halides, replacing the halide to give a new alkyne.

prompt: What organic product forms when sodium acetylide, HC≡C^− Na+, reacts with bromomethane, CH3Br?

choices.why: The acetylide carbon forms a new C–C bond to the methyl group rather than just picking up a proton.
The triple bond isn't touched. A new alkyl group attaches to the alkyne carbon.
Bromide leaves the alkyl halide; it doesn't bond to the alkyne. The methyl group bonds to the alkyne carbon instead.

explanation: The nucleophilic acetylide carbon forms a bond to the electrophilic carbon of bromomethane while Br^− departs. The new C–C bond gives propyne, and NaBr is the by-product.

prompt: In the reaction of acetylide anion with bromomethane, what happens as the new C–C bond forms?

choices.text: Br^− departs, taking with it the electron pair from the former C–Br bond
Br^− departs and leaves the C–Br electron pair on carbon
choices.why: Bromine leaves as bromide ion, so it takes both electrons of the old C–Br bond with it.

choices.text: The acetylide's triple bond becomes a double bond
choices.why: The triple bond isn't involved. The acetylide uses its lone pair to bond to carbon, and the product is still an alkyne.

choices.text: A methyl carbocation forms first, and the acetylide then adds to it
choices.why: In the section's picture, the new C–C bond forms at the same time as Br^− departs. No carbocation forms first.

explanation: Figure 9.8.1: the nucleophilic acetylide ion uses an electron pair to form a bond to the positively polarized, electrophilic carbon of bromomethane. As the new C–C bond forms, Br^− departs, taking the electron pair from the former C–Br bond, and propyne is the product.

prompt: Why is the reaction of an acetylide anion with an alkyl halide called an alkylation?

choices.text: A new alkyl group becomes attached to the starting alkyne
The alkyne is converted into an alkane
choices.why: The triple bond survives. The product is a new alkyne carrying an extra alkyl group.

choices.text: The alkyl halide loses HX to form an alkene
choices.why: That is elimination, which is what happens with secondary and tertiary halides instead of alkylation.

choices.text: The alkyne picks up the halogen from the alkyl halide
choices.why: The halide leaves as X^−. The alkyl group, not the halogen, attaches to the alkyne.

explanation: The acetylide replaces the halide of the alkyl halide and yields a new alkyne product. Because a new alkyl group has become attached to the starting alkyne, the reaction is called an alkylation.

prompt: 1-Hexyne is treated first with NaNH2 and then with 1-bromobutane. What is the product?

choices.why: The butyl group bonds to the former terminal carbon, so the triple bond ends up in the middle of the ten-carbon chain.
Alkylation doesn't reduce the triple bond. The product is still an alkyne.
Counting from either end, the triple bond joins C5 and C6, so its number is 5.

explanation: NaNH2 converts 1-hexyne into its acetylide anion, which displaces bromide from 1-bromobutane. The butyl group attaches to the former terminal carbon, giving CH3CH2CH2CH2C≡CCH2CH2CH2CH3, 5-decyne (76% in the section's example).

prompt: In the section's example, what percent yield of 5-decyne is obtained from 1-hexyne, NaNH2 and 1-bromobutane?
explanation: 1-Hexyne treated first with NaNH2 in NH3 and then with 1-bromobutane gives 5-decyne in 76% yield.

prompt: How can an internal alkyne, RC≡CR′, be made starting from acetylene?

choices.text: Alkylate acetylene to a terminal alkyne, then alkylate that alkyne again
Alkylate acetylene a single time with a secondary alkyl halide
choices.why: One alkylation gives only a terminal alkyne, and secondary halides give elimination rather than substitution.

choices.text: Alkylate an internal alkyne using NaNH2 and an alkyl halide
choices.why: An internal alkyne has no terminal hydrogen to remove, so it can't form an acetylide anion.

choices.text: Alkylate acetylene twice, using tertiary alkyl halides both times
choices.why: Tertiary alkyl halides undergo elimination with acetylide ions. Only primary alkyl bromides and iodides work.

explanation: Acetylide alkylation is a general way to build substituted alkynes. A terminal alkyne can be prepared by alkylation of acetylene itself, and an internal alkyne by further alkylation of a terminal alkyne. Each alkylation needs a primary alkyl bromide or iodide.

prompt: Which alkyl halides can be used to alkylate acetylide anions?

choices.text: Primary alkyl bromides and alkyl iodides

choices.why: With these, acetylide ions act as bases and cause elimination instead of substitution.

choices.text: Any alkyl halide, whether primary, secondary or tertiary
choices.why: Only primary alkyl bromides and iodides work. Secondary and tertiary halides undergo elimination.
Tertiary halides give elimination products with acetylide ions, not new alkynes.

explanation: The only limit to the alkylation reaction is that it can only use primary alkyl bromides and alkyl iodides. Acetylide ions are strong enough bases to cause elimination instead of substitution when they react with secondary and tertiary alkyl halides.

prompt: What happens when bromocyclohexane, a secondary alkyl halide, is treated with the propyne anion, CH3C≡C^−?

choices.why: That substitution product is not formed. The acetylide acts as a base toward the secondary halide.

choices.text: No reaction occurs, because the halide is secondary
choices.why: A reaction does occur, but it is elimination, giving cyclohexene.
No new C–C bond forms with this secondary halide; elimination happens instead.

explanation: Acetylide ions are strong bases. With a secondary halide such as bromocyclohexane, the propyne anion causes elimination, giving cyclohexene (and propyne) rather than the substitution product 1-cyclohexyl-1-propyne.

choices.why: A butyl group on propyne gives CH3C≡CCH2CH2CH2CH3, 2-heptyne, one carbon too many.
This gives CH3CH2C≡CCH2CH2CH3, which is 3-heptyne.
One alkylation of acetylene gives a terminal alkyne, here 1-hexyne. 2-Hexyne is an internal alkyne.

explanation: Alkylating the anion of propyne with 1-iodopropane joins CH3C≡C– to a propyl group, giving 2-hexyne. Exercise 9.8.1a also gives a second route: the anion of 1-pentyne with CH3I.

prompt: How many different terminal alkynes could serve as the starting alkyne for making 2-hexyne, CH3C≡CCH2CH2CH3, in one alkylation with a primary alkyl halide?
explanation: Either side of the triple bond can be the one supplied by the alkyl halide. 1-Pentyne + CH3I adds the methyl group, and propyne + CH3CH2CH2I adds the propyl group. Both halides are primary, so both routes are feasible (Exercise 9.8.1a).

prompt: Which starting materials would you use to make 2-methyl-3-hexyne, (CH3)2CHC≡CCH2CH3, by acetylide alkylation?

choices.why: 2-Iodopropane is a secondary halide, so the acetylide would cause elimination rather than substitution.
This joins a methyl and an isobutyl group to the triple bond, giving 5-methyl-2-hexyne, CH3C≡CCH2CH(CH3)2.
A methyl group gives (CH3)2CHC≡CCH3, 4-methyl-2-pentyne, one carbon short.

explanation: The triple bond has an isopropyl group on one side and an ethyl group on the other. Bringing in the isopropyl group from an alkyl halide would need a secondary halide, which gives elimination. So the isopropyl group must come from the terminal alkyne, 3-methyl-1-butyne, and the ethyl group from the primary halide CH3CH2I (Exercise 9.8.1b).

prompt: Which route gives 1-cyclohexyl-1-propyne, C6H11C≡CCH3 (a cyclohexane ring bonded to –C≡CCH3)?

choices.text: Cyclohexylacetylene, C6H11C≡CH, with NaNH2, then CH3I

choices.why: Bromocyclohexane is a secondary halide. The propyne anion causes elimination to cyclohexene instead.
An ethyl group gives C6H11C≡CCH2CH3, one carbon too many.

choices.text: Acetylene with NaNH2, then bromocyclohexane, then NaNH2 and CH3I
choices.why: The first alkylation fails: bromocyclohexane is secondary, so elimination gives cyclohexene.

explanation: The cyclohexyl group can't come from an alkyl halide, because bromocyclohexane is secondary and gives elimination (the section's own example). So it must already be on the terminal alkyne: the anion of cyclohexylacetylene plus CH3I gives 1-cyclohexyl-1-propyne (Exercise 9.8.1c).

prompt: How would you prepare cis-2-butene starting from propyne?

choices.text: NaNH2, then CH3I; then H2 over the Lindlar catalyst
NaNH2, then CH3I; then Li in liquid NH3
choices.why: Li/NH3 reduces 2-butyne to trans-2-butene.

choices.text: H2 over the Lindlar catalyst; then NaNH2, then CH3I
choices.why: Reducing first gives propene, which has no alkyne C–H. Alkenes are far too weakly acidic (ethylene's pK_a is 44) for NaNH2 to deprotonate, so no alkylation can follow.

choices.text: NaNH2, then CH3CH2I; then H2 over the Lindlar catalyst
choices.why: An ethyl group gives 2-pentyne, which is reduced to cis-2-pentene.

explanation: This needs two stages. Alkylating the anion of propyne with CH3I gives 2-butyne, CH3C≡CCH3, and syn hydrogenation over the Lindlar catalyst then gives cis-2-butene (Exercise 9.8.2).

prompt: Which alkyl halide would you treat with sodium acetylide to make 1-pentyne, HC≡CCH2CH2CH3?

choices.why: This secondary halide gives elimination with acetylide, and it would give a branched product anyway.
A butyl group on acetylene gives 1-hexyne, one carbon too many.
An ethyl group on acetylene gives 1-butyne, one carbon too few.

explanation: A terminal alkyne can be prepared by alkylation of acetylene itself. 1-Pentyne is HC≡C– joined to a propyl group, so the halide is the primary halide 1-bromopropane.
